dedupe_keys.name: liberia use of the new national emergency medical service in its first 22 months 2020 to 2022

description: This case study reviews how Liberia's national emergency medical service (EMS), created by the Ministry of Health in 2019, was used during its first 22 months. The authors, researchers at Emory University with partners including the Liberian Ministry of Health, analysed the monthly EMS dispatch report summaries from July 2020 to April 2022 and published the results in an open-access journal article. The data cover 4,494 calls nationwide, with call characteristics, chief complaints, the health district of each call and the receiving hospital. The article is free to read under a Creative Commons Attribution licence; the dispatch summaries themselves are not published. Caveats: the analysis is descriptive, relies on aggregated monthly reports, and covers the early start-up phase of the service. The study found that 89.3 percent of calls led to transport, most calls came from the Commonwealth and Central Monrovia districts of Montserrado County, John F. Kennedy Hospital in Monrovia received 42.6 percent of patients, and obstetric complaints (23.8 percent), infectious disease (17.4 percent) and road traffic injuries (7.6 percent) were the most common reasons. Simulation uses: demand and destination patterns for planning ambulance fleets, stations and hospital capacity in low-income countries building new prehospital systems. Related records: the Ankara ambulance demand study (case_study-ankara-ambulance-demand-forecasting-capacity-planning) addresses capacity planning in another setting.
